prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and market power in differentiated-product industries with endogenous prices, enabling empirical analysis of competition, mergers and welfare

statement.case_for: The random-coefficients demand framework, with Berry's inversion and equilibrium supply-side restrictions, solved a concrete identification and estimation problem: how to recover substitution patterns and markups when prices are endogenous and products are differentiated. It became a routine tool in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and it has spread to trade, health, environmental and public economics. The core work is about three decades old and has been tested through heavy use, including in regulatory practice. The BLP trio is a compact credit unit, because the central 1995 contribution is jointly authored and Berry's earlier inversion is part of it. That makes a three-person award easier to attribute than most competing candidates. A citation limited to demand estimation and market power can be defended without having to apportion the wider dynamic-games and production-function strands among many co-authors.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the award would honour a toolkit, and the Committee may weigh methods differently from substantive discoveries. The three-name cap also leaves out Bresnahan, who founded the new empirical IO programme and arguably did as much to define the agenda as Levinsohn did within BLP. A BLP-centred citation also leaves Pakes's dynamic-oligopoly and production-function work only partly covered, and credits Benkard, Reiss and Levin not at all. Finally, applied BLP results are known to be sensitive to numerical implementation and to instrument choice, so the reliability of the applications is more qualified than the method's wide adoption suggests.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first but names Bresnahan rather than Levinsohn as the third laureate, and sees Pakes as the central figure across the demand, production-function and dynamic-game strands.
responses.response: I take the Bresnahan case seriously, and in my opening I called him the most serious omission. My view is still that the citation should follow the discovery being rewarded. If it is about estimating demand and market power with endogenous prices, then Levinsohn is a co-author of the specific jointly authored result, and Bresnahan's contribution is the broader research programme and the earlier auto-industry work. Choosing Bresnahan would shift the citation toward the new empirical IO agenda, which is a defensible but different prize and one with a more diffuse attribution. I would reconsider if the Committee prefers the broader framing, but I would not treat it as a difference in merit between the two.

responses.point: Stromberg puts B001 first on originality, breadth and durability. He also flags that the Committee may see structural IO as methodological craft rather than discovery, and that the pooled candidate covers several distinct strands.
responses.response: I agree that the unit of the prize needs to be explicit, and I would answer the craft concern directly. The contribution is a measurement discovery, not only a technique, because it changed what economists can credibly say about substitution, markups and welfare in real markets. It also brought the same kind of discipline to settings far from IO. I would resolve the pooling problem by keeping the citation to demand estimation and market power. The dynamic-oligopoly and production-function work would stay as supporting context, and I would not try to credit every strand. That also answers Krusell's point about weighing Pakes's different strands.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B009 second, on the view that Persson, Tabellini and Besley built a coherent, well-attributed political-economics framework, and that the 2024 institutions prize is adjacent but addresses a different contribution.
responses.response: I largely share the view on attribution, and I ranked B009 second for that reason. I think the 2024 overlap is more than cosmetic, though. The institutions-and-prosperity prize covered closely related questions about how institutions shape economic outcomes, so a second award within a few years needs a clear argument for what is distinct. Persson-Tabellini on electoral rules and fiscal policy has that argument, but the cross-country identification is weaker than in B001, where the methods have been tested in practice. I therefore keep B009 as my first alternative and not as the lead candidate.

responses.point: Hassler treats the BLP trio as a clear, compact core and sees Bresnahan and Reiss as fitting a different strand. He ranks B049 second and B002 fourth, naming only Kiyotaki and Moore in B002.
responses.response: I agree on BLP and would add that Hassler's split between the BLP core and the broader empirical-IO strand supports a clean citation. On B002 I move somewhat toward his and Krusell's two-name framing. Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the collateral-amplification mechanism, and adding Gertler brings in the financial-accelerator line, which overlaps with the 2022 prize. I still ranked B002 below B001 and B009, but Hassler's argument makes it a more credible alternative than my opening rank of 6 implied, so I list it second among my alternatives. I do not move on B049, where attribution is too diffuse for a three-person cap.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would prefer Bresnahan to Levinsohn in the third position, and how it weighs the broader new empirical IO programme against the jointly authored BLP result.
Whether the Committee treats an estimation toolkit as a sufficient discovery, or wants a narrower or broader framing of the citation.
How far the dynamic-oligopoly and production-function work should be reflected in the citation if only Pakes of the three is credited for it.
I rely on background knowledge of the literature and have not independently verified citation, adoption or regulatory-use figures.
statement.conflict_note: Per my profile, I have no apparent connection to Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn. I work in industrial organisation and international trade, a neighbouring field, and I have tried to apply the common criteria and not a field preference. I have co-authored with Committee colleagues John Hassler and Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026). I am also married to Magdalena Andersson, a Swedish politician. The profile gives no evidence that either bears on this prize, so I disclose them without claiming a recusal need.
